description: Valois appanage duchy (1363–1477) that under Philip the Good and Charles the Bold assembled the Low Countries into a powerful Middle Kingdom between France and the Empire; its court was the cultural capital of northern Europe, source of Flemish painting, polyphonic music, and chivalric ceremony, before Charles the Bold's death at Nancy ended the Burgundian project.

temporal.notes: Valois cadet branch; Charles the Bold's death at Nancy ends independent state

lifecycle_phases.description: Philip the Bold (1363–1404), younger brother of the French king Charles V, receives Burgundy as an appanage and builds it into a powerful state. Through marriage to Margaret of Flanders (1369), he acquires the richest manufacturing region in northern Europe. John the Fearless (1404–1419) is assassinated at Montereau, an event that drives Burgundy into alliance with England during the Hundred Years' War.

Philip the Good (1419–1467) creates a quasi-independent state between France and the Holy Roman Empire. The Treaty of Troyes (1420), in which Burgundy supports the English claim to France, nearly destroys the French monarchy. Philip founds the Order of the Golden Fleece (1430), the most prestigious chivalric order in Europe. His court at Bruges and Dijon is the center of northern European art (van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden).

Charles the Bold (1467–1477) attempts to create a contiguous kingdom between his northern (Flanders) and southern (Burgundy) territories by conquering Lorraine and Switzerland. Three catastrophic defeats against Swiss infantry (Grandson, Murten, Nancy, 1476–1477) end with Charles killed at Nancy. Louis XI of France seizes the Burgundian duchy; the Habsburg Maximilian I marries Charles's daughter Mary and inherits the Netherlands, splitting the inheritance.

rise_factors.description: Flemish and Brabantine cloth industries, the most productive manufacturing sector in Europe, made Burgundy's northern territories the wealthiest region north of the Alps; wool imports from England, dye from the Mediterranean, and Flemish technical skill created export earnings that funded the most lavish court in Europe

The Valois-Burgundy dukes accumulated territory through marriage rather than conquest: Philip the Bold's marriage brought Flanders, while subsequent marriages added Artois, Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland; this diplomatic accumulation created a territorial mass without exhausting military resources

Burgundian vineyards (Côte d'Or, Chablis) produced the most valued wines in northern Europe. Ecclesiastical landowners, Cistercian and Benedictine abbeys, systematized viticulture, generating wine revenues that funded ducal patronage.

Philip the Bold (1363–1404) received Burgundy from the French crown but used marriage (to the heiress of Flanders) to accumulate the Low Countries' commercial and financial resources, transforming a French duchy into a European power.

Burgundian court patronage supported Flemish painting (van Eyck, van der Weyden) and polyphonic music (Dufay, Binchois), making the duchy the cultural capital of 15th-century northern Europe and a model for aristocratic display.

The inheritance of Flanders (1384) gave Burgundy control of Europe's most productive cloth industry. Ghent, Bruges, and Ypres employed tens of thousands in textile production, generating revenues that dwarfed the French royal treasury.

decline_factors.description: Charles the Bold's attempt to conquer Lorraine and Switzerland to connect his northern and southern territories fatally overextended Burgundian military power; Swiss pike infantry proved superior to Burgundian heavy cavalry in mountain terrain

Charles the Bold's death without a male heir allowed France to claim the core duchy under Salic law; his daughter Mary's marriage to Maximilian Habsburg split the inheritance and ended Burgundy's independent existence

Charles the Bold's military disasters at Grandson (1476), Murten (1476), and Nancy (1477) against the Swiss Confederation destroyed the Burgundian army. His death at Nancy ended the male line and triggered French absorption of Burgundy proper.

Louis XI of France immediately claimed Burgundy upon Charles's death (1477) by feudal reversion law. Despite Flemish and Hapsburg resistance, France absorbed the duchy itself, leaving the Low Countries to Habsburg control.
